reason: Confirmed by driving, not by reading. At 390x844 with touch the strip is 308px wide, so the axis runs at 6.84px/day and the de-swarm (MIN=16, 15px row pitch) puts the 3-day and 6-day marks on row 1 directly up-and-right of the 2-day and 5-day marks on row 0. Measured centres: dot0 (54.7,1856.3) vs dot1 (61.5,1841.3) is dx 6.8, dy 15, euclidean 16.47px; dot2 vs dot3 is dx 6.9, euclidean 16.51px. The .dot::after expander is inset -11px on all four sides on a 12px disc, i.e. a circle of radius 17px, so both row-0 centres fall inside their row-1 neighbour's expander by roughly half a pixel, and the row-1 dot is later in DOM order with no z-index anywhere, so it paints and hit-tests on top. document.elementFromPoint at each mark's own centre returns [1,1,3,3,4,5,6,7,8] - dots 0 and 2 never resolve to themselves. A real touchscreen tap at the exact centre of dot0 raises '3 days open / Confirm the Harbour wall cordon with the harbourmaster'; at the centre of dot2 it raises '6 days open / Approve the final seating plan'. Identical on full, partial, quiet and first-run. Self-ownership of those two marks' own expander area measures 28.9% and 35.5% (the seat said 32% and 43% - it understates the theft slightly, not in its favour). Neither gate catches it: interaction-check.mjs line 247 asserts hypot of centres >= 12 and reports 16px here, which is true and irrelevant; audit.mjs line 389 flags only min(w,h) < 28 on the union of box and pseudo, which is size, not stacking order. Does not reproduce at 768 (566px strip, 12.6px/day, nearest cross-row pair 19.6px > 17), 1280 or 1440, so this is a 390-only defect - correctly scoped by the seat. Two corrections to the write-up that do not change the verdict: the affected marks are not 'uninspectable at all by pointer' - 29% and 36% of their expander still resolves to them, so a tap low or left of the disc does reach them; and keyboard travel and the .sr fallback paragraph both still name all nine jobs with their ages, so this is a sighted-touch failure specifically. Severity holds at misleading, not blocking: seven of nine marks work, so the capability is not gone, but the product silently answers with a different job's title and a different day count on the one surface where that tooltip is the only place either appears, and nothing on screen signals the mismatch. That is an untrue assertion delivered confidently, which is exactly the misleading class.
sharpenedFix: The proposed fix is correct and its arithmetic checks out against the real source - I applied it in the browser and re-measured. MIN 16->20, .dot { bottom: calc(20px + var(--row, 0) * 20px); }, strip.style.minHeight = `${92 + Math.max(0, rows.length - 1) * 20}px`, and .dot::after { top: -8px; right: -11px; bottom: -8px; left: -11px; }. After it: every mark's centre resolves to itself at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440 in both full and partial (elementFromPoint returns [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8] everywhere); the audit target union measures 34x28 on every dot, so min(w,h) = 28 and the `< 28` floor still passes; closest-pair rises to 20.53px at 390, well over the behaviour gate's 12px; all marks still sit inside the strip. The guarantee is structural rather than data-dependent: MIN=20 makes same-row separation at least 20px against a 17px half-width, and the 14px half-height cannot reach a 20px row pitch. Two tightenings worth folding in. First, note that border-radius: 999px on a 34x28 box yields an ellipse, so the corners of that nominal rect are not tappable even though audit.mjs measures the rect - if you want the measured 28px to be the real 28px, set .dot::after { border-radius: 14px; } instead of 999px, which changes nothing visible (the pseudo is transparent) and makes the hit region a true stadium. Second, since the 28px floor is now met with exactly zero margin, add an explicit assertion to interaction-check.mjs rather than relying on audit.mjs: for every .dot, elementFromPoint at its own centre must resolve to itself, run at 390 and 1440. Without that, this class walks straight back in the next time the pitch or the expander is touched, because the existing closest-pair rule is structurally blind to occlusion.
